fact_sheet.business_description: The company operates a social network that enables users to maintain identity, relationships, messages, photographs and shared content [D01]. Advertisers pay the company to reach targeted audiences on this platform [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Social networking platform sold to users for connection/communication and to advertisers for targeted reach [D01].
Value proposition includes habitual engagement and a social graph that is difficult to replicate [D01].
economics: Advertising supplied approximately 85% of 2011 revenue, with payments and other fees supplying the remainder [D01].
Large advertising platform model features significant operating leverage, as incremental ad impressions do not require additional physical stores [D01].
No maintenance-capex split or normalized owner-earnings estimate provided [D02].
earnings_record: 2011 revenue was $3.711 billion with $1.000 billion net income; 2010 revenue was $1.974 billion with $606 million net income [D01].
First-quarter 2012 revenue was $1.058 billion vs $731 million in Q1 2011; net income was $205 million vs $233 million in Q1 2011 [D01].
competitive_position: 901 million monthly active users and 526 million daily active users as of March 31, 2012 [D01].
Moat is evidenced by habitual engagement and a difficult-to-replicate social graph [D01].
Competes with other social services for time and Google for digital advertising [D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Gross IPO proceeds are not all retained corporate cash; a significant portion of the offer consists of secondary shares [D01].
No specific debt or leverage figures provided in the pack [D02].
management_and_capital_allocation: Zuckerberg is expected to control approximately 55.9% of the voting power after the offering [D01].
Class A has one vote per share, Class B has ten votes per share [D01].
price_and_valuation: Implied fully diluted equity value is approximately $104 billion [D02].
Implied valuation is roughly 104 times 2011 net income, representing a 0.96% historical earnings yield [D02].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Mobile use grows faster than mobile monetization [D05].
First-quarter profit fell despite revenue growth [D05].
Risks regarding user preferences, privacy restrictions, competitors, and platform dependency [D05].
Dual-class voting structure limits minority shareholder control [D05].
deal_terms_if_any: Offer consists of 421,233,615 Class A shares at $38 per share, including 180 million newly issued shares and 241,233,615 secondary shares [D01].
recent_events: April 2012: The company announced an agreement to acquire 'the Company' [D07].
May 17, 2012: Final prospectus issued setting the $38 offering price [D07].
berkshire_context: Berkshire had approximately $37.3 billion in cash and equivalents and $77 billion in equity investments as of the 2011 annual report [D08].
No issuer-specific Buffett verdict provided in the pack [D08].
missing_data: Maintenance capital expenditure figures, normalized owner earnings, and comprehensive debt/leverage details.

understandable.evidence: Rapid technological change and shifting user preferences in the social media space make it impossible to say with confidence what the business will look like in 10-20 years [D01], [D05].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: While the company has a large network, it faces intense competition for user time and advertising dollars, and the durability of its moat against changing preferences is unproven [D01], [D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: The company has a short operating history and recently experienced a decline in net income despite revenue growth in the first quarter of 2012 [D01], [D05].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The pack lacks sufficient data on debt, leverage, and maintenance capital requirements to determine the true return on tangible capital [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The platform model exhibits significant operating leverage as incremental users do not require additional physical infrastructure [D01].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: The dual-class voting structure, which provides 55.9% control to a single individual, limits the rights of minority shareholders and is inconsistent with our standards [D01], [D05].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: At an equity value of roughly $104 billion, the company is large enough to move the needle for Berkshire [D02].

price_screen.evidence: The implied earnings yield is approximately 0.96%, far below our 10% pre-tax threshold [D02].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a high-growth but unproven technology platform with significant management concentration and an exorbitant price.

gate2.why_available: The market is pricing the company based on high expectations for future growth, while we view the current valuation as disconnected from fundamentals due to an exorbitant price [D02]. We find the business lacks the predictable, long-term earnings track record and owner-minded governance required for our investment, making the current high price tag unjustified regardless of growth prospects [D01], [D05].
evidence: Implied valuation is roughly 104 times 2011 net income, representing a 0.96% historical earnings yield [D02].

gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market appears to be discounting the significant risks regarding user preferences, competition, and the inability to effectively monetize mobile engagement, while accepting the dual-class voting structure as a trade-off for growth [D05].

A shift in governance to protect minority shareholder rights
A valuation that provides a significant margin of safety based on current owner earnings

key_assumptions: Maintenance capex assumed to be a significant portion of current spend [D02]

gate3.price_vs_value: Price is 104x earnings; no margin of safety exists [D02]
gate3.alternatives: Existing holdings or Berkshire buyback; current market price represents a poor capital allocation relative to our required return threshold [D02], [D08]
gate3.downside_case: Significant risk of capital impairment if user engagement shifts or monetization fails to scale; permanent loss is possible [D05]

gate4.role_description: permanent_passive_holder — value realised by the business compounding and rational capital allocation; Berkshire's edge is patience and permanent capital [D08].
value_realisation_path: value is realised through the long-term compounding of the business's intrinsic value and capital allocation decisions [D08].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: For marketable securities post-1980, we act as a permanent, passive holder of businesses we understand, allowing the economics of the company to compound over time [D08].

kill_criteria: Pricing power eroded by shifting user preferences or platform irrelevance [D01], [D06]
Management fails to address mobile monetization or experiences sustained earnings decline [D05]
Regulatory or privacy changes significantly restrict ad targeting capabilities [D05]
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Maintain liquidity above the $30B cash floor; avoid non-controlling stakes that lack long-term governance alignment [D08]
gate5.opportunity_cost: Capital is better deployed into existing high-quality businesses or repurchasing undervalued Berkshire stock [D08]
gate5.decider_reason: The business operates outside my circle of competence due to rapid technological change and lacks the historical earnings consistency required for a core position.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: We risk permanent loss of capital because the current valuation is untethered from owner earnings and the competitive moat is unproven against rapidly changing social media preferences.

The company lacks a long-term, consistent record of earnings, with net income recently declining despite revenue growth [D01], [D05].

final.what_would_change_our_mind: A decade of consistent, high returns on capital, a change in governance to align with minority shareholders, and a valuation that provides a significant margin of safety based on normalized owner earnings.
final.memo:
The Company operates a social platform that has achieved significant scale, yet it remains a business we find impossible to value with the precision we require [D01], [D02]. While it connects millions of users and generates advertising revenue, the rapid pace of technological change and shifting consumer preferences make it a guessing game to predict its competitive position ten or twenty years from now [D01], [D05], [D06].

We look for durable moats, but here the sustainability of the company's network is unproven against competitors vying for the same limited user time and advertising budgets [D01], [D06]. Furthermore, the company's recent financial performance has been inconsistent, showing a decline in net income despite revenue growth, which leaves us unable to gain confidence in its long-term economics [D01], [D05].

Our standard for management is simple: we want able and honest individuals who act like owners. A dual-class voting structure that vests 55.9% of control in one person is an institutional imperative we cannot accept [D01]. We require governance that treats all shareholders as partners, not as outsiders to the inner sanctum of control [D01].

At a valuation of 104 times 2011 earnings, the market is offering a 0.96% initial yield [D02]. This price is untethered from reality. We would rather sit on our cash than pay an exorbitant price for a business that lacks the predictable, long-term earnings track record we demand [D02], [D05], [D08]. We will pass and continue waiting for opportunities that meet our standards.
